notes: M2 Intro beat. Marcus Webb — the player's campaign manager — delivers his first operational report. Where Petra Solis reads the player, Marcus reads the board. Tone: transactional, data-driven, no sentimentality. Purpose: establish Marcus's voice, introduce the Corporate Lobby as an early-game pressure vector, and hand off the briefing document that unlocks Marcus's recurring advice mechanic. Diamond structure (converge at faction-warning, branch at warning-detail). No ideology-drift effects authored — OQ-2 pending Sol; flag effects only. Faction ID 'corporate-lobby' is an authoring placeholder pending Nova's FactionSystem spec. voiceTag 'machine-boss' is the closest available archetype; Marcus is not a Whip but runs the same transactional register — TODO(vex/OQ-E): confirm whether a dedicated 'campaign-fixer' voiceTag is warranted or whether 'machine-boss' covers this character class. Player choice at open-b is characterization (no mechanical delta); player choice at warning-detail is strategic positioning (flag-observable by future Corporate Lobby events). New character: Marcus Webb not in GDD §12.3.4 named seed list — TODO(vex): Jesse to create wiki entry.

open.speaker: marcus-webb
open.text: Senator {pc.name}. Marcus Webb. Before you ask — no, I don't do congratulations.

open-b.speaker: marcus-webb
open-b.text: You came in at forty-one percent favorable, thirty-seven unfavorable, twenty-two undecided. That's your baseline. Everything I do is about the twenty-two.

options.label: Forty-one to start is workable. What's the path to fifty?
I didn't run on polling averages.
You've already run the scenarios. You're reciting from memory.
options.failureHint: Requires Strategy 3. You haven't learned to read a briefing room yet.

response-numbers.speaker: marcus-webb
response-numbers.text: Good. You understand the problem. The path is legislation that moves, not legislation that impresses.

response-vision.speaker: marcus-webb
response-vision.text: Vision speeches are for donors. The chamber runs on schedules and favors. We can revisit vision after you have fifty-one votes.

response-test.speaker: marcus-webb
response-test.text: Four scenarios. You came in on a Wednesday, so I had an extra day. The comfortable read is a problem you don't have yet.

faction-warning.speaker: marcus-webb
faction-warning.text: There's one variable that isn't in the polling and will consume your first six months if you ignore it.

warning-detail.speaker: marcus-webb
warning-detail.text: The Corporate Lobby. They don't want to own you — they want optionality. They'll be in your office by end of week with a modest ask. It won't feel like a test. It is.

options.label: I'm not taking industry meetings in my first month.
I can defer and keep the door open.
If they want optionality, they can pay for it.

response-fight.speaker: marcus-webb
response-fight.text: They'll note the closed door and file it. Don't be surprised when their money goes to your primary challenger instead. Might still be the right call.

response-avoid.speaker: marcus-webb
response-avoid.text: Deferring is a signal too. They'll read it as soft. Take the meeting when it comes — just make them talk first.

response-leverage.speaker: marcus-webb
response-leverage.text: Now you're thinking like a manager. Don't say that out loud again until you know the room.

briefing.speaker: marcus-webb
briefing.text: I put together a briefing document. Faction breakdown, committee calendar, your first three months mapped against the legislative clock. Read it before tomorrow.

exit.speaker: narrator
exit.text: Webb sets a folder on the desk and leaves without waiting for a response.
